title: Parts I to IV (overview, lexical, grammar, types)

found.group: G1: Parts I to IV (overview, lexical, grammar, types)

findings.title: `Self` as a parameter type is not excluded from a `dyn`-usable interface
findings.program:
interface Same:
    fn same(other: Self) -> bool          # has an object, returns no Self, not generic: usable as dyn by [TYP-22]

struct Tag implements Same:
    id: i64
    fn same(other: Tag) -> bool: return this.id == other.id

struct Name implements Same:
    text: String
    fn same(other: Name) -> bool: return this.text == other.text

fn both(a: dyn Same, b: dyn Same) -> bool:
    return a.same(b)                       # <-- BREAKS: `other` is `Self`, which a `dyn Same` cannot name; the table entry for `Tag` reads the `Name`'s bytes (a String header) as a `Tag`

fn main():
    println(both(Tag(id=1), Name(text="x")))
findings.why: [TYP-22]: "An interface is usable as `dyn` only if every method has an object (none is a `static fn`), does not return `Self` by value (methods marked `where Self: needs Sized` excepted), and is not generic, except over a type parameter used only as the type of a parameter that views its value". Nothing speaks of `Self` as a parameter's type, and nothing says what `Self` is on a `dyn I` receiver; an implementer who takes it as `dyn I` (the only type available) lets a value of one kind be read as another. [TYP-36] shows the authors know the problem for `Eq` ("`owns dyn I` compares when `I` requires `Eq` ... values of two different kinds are never equal", a special table entry), but the rule for a direct call stays silent.
findings.proposed_text: Replace in `[TYP-22]`: "An interface is usable as `dyn` only if every method has an object (none is a `static fn`), does not return `Self` by value (methods marked `where Self: needs Sized` excepted), and is not generic, ..." with: "An interface is usable as `dyn` only if every method has an object (none is a `static fn`), names `Self` nowhere but as `this`: not as a result by value, and not as a parameter's type or inside one (`fn eq(other: Self)`, `fn add(rhs: Self)`, `fn merge(owns other: Self)`), since through a `dyn I` value the kind of any other value is unknown (methods marked `where Self: needs Sized` excepted, which a `dyn` value does not have), and is not generic, ...". Add to the `E2050` examples: "`Same` cannot be used as `dyn Same`: `same` takes `other: Self`, and through a `dyn Same` the kind of `other` is unknown; take `other: dyn Same` and test its kind in the body, `if other is Tag as o:`, or mark `same` with `where Self: needs Sized` and call it on the concrete types". Keep `[TYP-36]`'s entry for `owns dyn I` where `I: needs Eq` (the kinds are compared first) and say there that it is the one way `Eq` is reached through `dyn`.
findings.codes: E2050 (reused), shape as today: names the method and gives the line to write

findings.title: `n as Color`: an integer cast to a unit-only enum, which the text calls "an integer"
findings.program:
enum Color:
    Red
    Green

fn show(c: Color):
    match c:                   # exhaustive by [ENM-2]: two arms
        Red: println("r")
        Green: println("g")

fn main():
    c = 7 as Color             # <-- BREAKS: [TYP-12] "a unit-only enum is an integer", [TYP-6] "integer → integer: keeps the low bits"; 7 is no variant
    show(c)                    # a jump table indexed by 7, or `Option[Color]` reading `None` ([TYP-13]): an invalid value in Safe code
    o: Option[Color] = Some(c)
findings.why: [TYP-12]: "A unit-only enum is an integer (`@repr(u8)` and friends choose it; the default is the smallest signed type that fits)". [TYP-6]: "`x as T` converts explicitly: integer → integer: keeps the low bits (truncation or sign/zero extension)". Read together they admit `7 as Color`. [TYP-6] also says nothing of `bool` with `as` (`true as int`), so an implementer guesses there too. [TYP-13] gives an enum with unused discriminants a niche, so the invalid value also corrupts `Option[Color]`.
findings.proposed_text: In `[TYP-12]` replace "A unit-only enum is an integer" with "A unit-only enum is stored as an integer". Add to `[TYP-6]`'s list: "* `bool → integer`: `true` is 1 and `false` 0; nothing converts to `bool` (`x != 0` is the test); * a unit-only enum → an integer type that holds every one of its discriminants (`Color.Green as u8`); an integer never converts to an enum: a value of an enum is one of its variants (`[TYP-12]`) and `Option[Color]` keeps `None` in an unused discriminant (`[TYP-13]`), so `7 as Color` is `E2020` ("an integer may be no `Color`; write `Color.try_from(7)`, a `Result[Color, RangeError]`, and open its `Ok`"). * `as` between any other pair of types is `E2020` naming both."
findings.codes: E2020 (reused), the mismatched-types shape with the `try_from` line as its help

findings.title: A value `using A` keeps its instance's address, which no marker and no race rule sees
findings.program:
from std.mem import Arena          # a one-thread bump arena implementing Allocator ([ALC-2]); allocate bumps a pointer in `this`

fn fill(ref mut current: Arena):
    xs: Array[int] using Arena = Array.new_in(current)
    ys: Array[int] using Arena = Array.new_in(current)
    thread.scope(fn(ref mut s):
        s.spawn(fn() owns xs:                       # <-- BREAKS: `Array[int]` is `Send` ("every component is", int is); the kept instance word is no component the table names
            for i in 0..1_000_000: xs.push(i))      #     each growth calls `current.allocate(...)` on the task's thread ...
        for i in 0..1_000_000: ys.push(i))          #     ... while this thread does the same: two threads bump one pointer; [THR-11] sees no place both tasks change

fn main():
    current = Arena(1 << 24)
    fill(ref mut current)
findings.why: [TYP-46]: "A value whose manager may have several instances keeps its instance's address, one word, so that its growth and its end go back to the instance it came from"; "takes the value's block from it by calling `current.allocate(...)`". [THR-8]/the marker table: "`Send` ... inferred: every component is `Send`"; neither names the instance word as a component, nor says whether it is a view (`ref A`), a link or a raw pointer. [THR-11] checks "one place" two tasks change; nothing says the growth of `xs` is a change of `current`. The same for `thread_shared T using A`: its end may run on another thread ([RC-4], F10) and calls `deallocate` on a one-thread instance.
findings.proposed_text: Add to `[TYP-46]` (and the same sentence to `[ALC-1]`): "The instance word a value keeps is a view of its instance, `ref A`, for every rule of the language: the value is `Send` or `ThreadShared` only when `A` is `ThreadShared` (`[THR-8]`, `[THR-9]`), since its growth and its end call `allocate` and `deallocate` on the instance from whichever thread holds it; and each growth and each end of the value is a call of those methods on the instance through that view, which the exclusivity and race rules see as they see any call (`[BRW-21]`, `[THR-11]`): two scoped tasks growing values made in one `Arena` are `E7007`, naming the arena, unless `Arena.allocate` synchronises inside (`A: ThreadShared`). A `thread_shared T using A`, and a value `using A` handed to another thread, with an `A` that is not `ThreadShared` is `E7015` ("`xs` takes its memory from `current`, an `Arena`, which one thread uses at a time; make it in the built-in manager, `xs = []`, or use a manager that any thread may call"). A manager with one instance is reached through no word and is judged by its own `static` state (`[STA-1]`, `[THR-20]`)." Add `ref A` for `using A` values to the marker table's `Send` and `ThreadShared` rows.
findings.codes: E7015 and E7007 (reused), each with the help line above
findings.touches_owner_verdict: 107 (the instance word; the proposal keeps verdict 107's two exceptions and adds only what the word is for the markers)

findings.title: `base_type` admits every stack of words; the text defines each word alone
findings.program:
struct Slot:
    item: shares mut ref mut Item       # base_type := "shares" ["mut"] base_type; base_type := "ref" ["mut"] base_type: grammatical
    keep: owns owns Mesh
    back: thread_shared shares Node
    view: owns ref String

fn main():
    it = Item(hp=1)
    a = shares mut Slot(item=ref mut it)  # which rule decides whether two `shares mut` owners may each write through the one `ref mut`? [BRW-1] speaks of names; both are one name's copies
    b = shares mut a
    a.item.hp = 2
    println(b.item.hp)
findings.why: III.3: "`base_type := path_type | "ref" ["mut"] base_type | "sharedref" "mut" base_type | "owns" base_type | "shares" ["mut"] base_type | "thread_shared" base_type | "weakref" base_type | ..." is recursive on every word. [TYP-45]: "A type says how its value is held, with the word on the type it describes" and then defines `T`, `owns T`, `shares T`, ..., each with `T` a plain type. [TYP-15] ("A view may be stored in any place") lets a reader take `owns ref T` and `shares ref mut T` as defined; IV.11 strips "one level" of `owns`, which presumes a second may exist. O2 names one pair (`weakref shares T`) and nothing names the rest. An implementer must decide which stacks are types and what each one's owner, region and `Send` are.
findings.proposed_text: * `[TYP-45a]` **One word on a type.** A word of `[TYP-45]` stands before a type that has no word of its own: a `path_type`, a tuple, a fixed array, a function type or a `dyn` bound (`owns Mesh`, `shares mut Player`, `weakref Node`, `ref Span[int]`, `owns dyn Shape`, `thread_shared fn()`). `ref` and `ref mut` also stand before a type with a word, as the view of a place that holds such a value (`ref mut owns Mesh` is what `ref mut lvl.mesh` names; `[TYP-14]` reads through it, and `=` on it replaces the block as `=` on the field does). Every other word before a word (`owns ref T`, `shares mut ref mut T`, `owns owns T`, `owns shares T`, `thread_shared shares T`, `weakref shares T`; `weakref thread_shared T` is O2's) is `E0100`: "`shares mut ref mut Item` stacks two words; a counted block holds a value of its own: write `shares mut Item`, or, for one view that several names may change, `sharedref mut Item`". A value that is to hold a view is a struct with a view field (`[TYP-34]`), and one that is to hold a link is a struct with a link field.
findings.codes: E0100 (reused), the help giving the type with one word

findings.title: How a type index is assigned across separately compiled packages is unsaid
findings.program:
# package `shapes`, compiled once ([BLD-1]):
open class Shape:
    pass
class Circle(Shape):
    r: float = 1.0
pub fn radius(s: Shape) -> float:
    return (cast s as Circle).r          # one compare of type indices ([TYP-44]): against the index `shapes` gave `Circle`

# package `app`, which depends on `shapes`:
class Square(Shape):
    side: float = 2.0
fn main():
    println(shapes.radius(Square()))     # <-- if each package numbers its own types from 1, `Square` may carry `Circle`'s number; the cast passes and reads a Square as a Circle
findings.why: [TYP-44]: "Each test and each cast is one compare of type indices." [OBJ-1]: "The header is 8 bytes: a 32-bit count and a 32-bit type index". [MNG-4] names type information `em_ti_…` as a symbol; [MONO-1] deduplicates instances at link time. No rule says who gives the 32-bit number, when, or that two types in one process never share one; a dependant's kinds, a reload image's new kinds (Annex B) and a generic instance deduplicated from two packages all need one. The natural per-package numbering is the unsafe guess.
findings.proposed_text: * `[TYP-44a]` **One index per type in a process.** A type index is a number no two types in one process share, given when the program is linked (and, for a reload image, when it is loaded, `[HR-12a]`), never when a package is compiled: compiled code names a type by its type-information symbol (`em_ti_…`, `[MNG-4]`), the linker gives each symbol its index and fills every compare with it, and a generic instance deduplicated at link (`[MONO-1]`) has one index. A kind test or cast is then one compare of the header's index against a constant (`[COST-3]`); a C toolchain that cannot fill an immediate from a link-time value loads the constant once per function, which `ember inspect` reports as that row. Two packages that give two types one index are refused at link (`E9035`'s shape, naming both types).
findings.codes: E9035 (reused: packages of one process disagree) or a new E904x if the registry wants a row of its own

findings.title: A `#!` line after an import: a comment by [LEX-10], `E0104` by [GRM-37]
findings.why: [LEX-10]: "A line beginning `#!` before the first import or item is a directive (`[GRM-37]`), not a comment; anywhere else it is a comment." [GRM-37]: "A directive after an import or item, an unknown directive, or a module attribute with an invalid target or arguments is `E0104`." The two disagree on the same line, and [LEX-10]'s reading lets `#! module overflow(wrap)` be accepted and ignored.
findings.proposed_text: Replace in `[LEX-10]`: "A line beginning `#!` before the first import or item is a directive (`[GRM-37]`), not a comment; anywhere else it is a comment." with: "A line beginning `#!` is a directive wherever it stands (`[GRM-37]`), never a comment: one below an import or an item is `E0104` ("`#! module overflow(wrap)` is a directive, and directives come first; move it above `import std.io`"). The one exception is a shebang line (G1-18)."

findings.title: The `file` production has no statements, which the entry file may hold
findings.program:
# the entry file ([GRM-2]):
import std.io
x = 5
fn double(n: int) -> int: return n * 2     # "items anywhere in the file are declared as usual" ([FN-8])
println(double(x))
import std.math                              # may an import follow a statement? the grammar says no; no rule says what it is
findings.why: III.1: "`file := {directive} {NEWLINE} {import_decl} {item}`" and the Part's own claim, "Every construct used anywhere in this specification appears here". [GRM-2]: "in the entry file only ... statements at file scope, which form the implicit `main`"; [FN-8]: "the statements at file scope of the entry file form, in source order, the body of an implicit `fn main()` ...; items anywhere in the file are declared as usual". The production cannot parse the file [FN-8] describes, and nothing says whether an import may follow a statement or an item.
findings.proposed_text: Replace the production with: "`file := {directive} {NEWLINE} {import_decl} {item | statement}   -- `statement` in the entry file only ([GRM-2]); elsewhere E0100`". Add to `[GRM-2]`: "Items and statements of the entry file stand in any order; the statements, in source order, are `main`'s body (`[FN-8]`). An import below an item or a statement is `E0100` ("imports come first: move `import std.math` above line 2")."

findings.title: Bidirectional format characters in source: the reviewer reads one program, the compiler another
findings.program:
# a dependency's source, or its overlay ([GRM-35]), read by a reviewer before the build:
fn check(p: *i32) -> bool:
    # SAFETY: p is checked by the caller⁦‮ }  # ⁦ if p is None: return false   <-- BREAKS: U+202E/U+2066 (Trojan Source, CVE-2021-42574) make the comment display as code and code as comment; [LEX-11] says a comment never produces a diagnostic
    unsafe:
        return *p == 0
findings.why: [LEX-1]: "Source files are UTF-8. A byte-order mark is accepted and ignored ... An invalid UTF-8 sequence is `E0001`" — U+202A–U+202E and U+2066–U+2069 are valid UTF-8. [LEX-11]: "a comment never affects compilation, including by producing a diagnostic." [LEX-26] lists what a literal admits by escapes, not which raw characters. No rule names the bidirectional controls, so a dependency or an overlay (whose facts the compiler trusts, `[FFI-2]`) can show a reviewer a program other than the one lexed, against `[PHIL-16]` ("The words say what the code does").
findings.proposed_text: * `[LEX-1a]` A Unicode bidirectional format character (U+202A to U+202E, U+2066 to U+2069) anywhere in a source file, an overlay or a manifest, in a comment or a string literal included, is `E0010` ("line 3 holds U+202E, which reorders how the line is shown; write the text as an escape, `\u{202E}`, inside the literal, or remove it"); the one way to put one in a program is the escape of `[LEX-26]`. This is the one diagnostic a comment produces (`[LEX-11]`).
findings.codes: new code E0010 (none registered; the first pass added none, so `codes.rs`'s test and XVII.9 gain one row)

findings.title: A lambda with an indented block body outside brackets: grammatical, and the prose does not say
findings.program:
fn main():
    total = 0
    count = 0
    h = fn(x):              # lambda := ... (":" block); block := NEWLINE INDENT {statement} DEDENT: parses
        total += x
        count += 1          # [GRM-17] speaks only of a body "on the lambda's own line"; [LEX-6a] says a body of more than one statement is a local function
    h(1)
findings.why: III.5: "`lambda := [...] "fn" "(" ... ")" [capture_list] ["->" type] ("=>" expression | ":" block)`" with `block := NEWLINE INDENT {statement} DEDENT | simple_stmt NEWLINE`. [GRM-17]: "Outside brackets, a `:` body on the lambda's own line is one simple statement, ended by the statement's `NEWLINE`"; [LEX-6a]: "A lambda body needing more than one statement is written as a local function." The grammar accepts what the prose implies is written another way, and `E0106`'s registry row says "cannot be written inside brackets" only.
findings.proposed_text: Replace in the grammar: `("=>" expression | ":" block)` with `("=>" expression | ":" simple_stmt)`, and in `[GRM-17]`: "A lambda's `:` body is one simple statement, inside brackets (`[LEX-6a]`) and outside alike; a `NEWLINE` and `INDENT` after the `:` is `E0106`, whose help declares a local function on the line above (`fn add(x):` with the block, then `h = add`, `[GRM-28]`)." In XVII.9, `E0106`: "a lambda body of more than one statement, or an indented block after a lambda's `:`".

findings.title: One-element tuples: values and types the grammar makes, which [TYP-27] refuses
findings.why: [TYP-27]: "Written as a type, `()` is `void`: a tuple type has two or more elements (ODR-071)." [GRM-29]: "An `expr_list` ... of one expression followed by a comma, is a tuple"; [GRM-38]: "`(e,)` a tuple". So `(5,)` is a value of a type that does not exist. Verdict 115 records the owner calling `(A,)` "a tuple `[TYP-27]` refuses".
findings.proposed_text: Grammar: `tuple_lit := "(" ")" | "(" expression "," expression {"," expression} [","] ")"` and `tuple_type := "(" ")" | "(" type "," type {"," type} [","] ")"`. In `[GRM-29]` and `[GRM-38]` replace "`(e,)` a tuple" with "`(e,)` is `E0100` ("a tuple has two or more elements; write `e`, or `(e, ())` for a pair"); in a `return` or an `expr_list`, a trailing comma after one expression is the same".

findings.title: Upcast of a `shares`, `thread_shared` or `weakref` class value to its base is unsaid
findings.program:
open class Animal:
    pass
class Dog(Animal):
    pass

fn main():
    d = shares mut Dog()
    a: shares mut Animal = shares mut d   # rule 8 lists "a class object to a base class (upcast)" and the dyn forms with their words; not `shares mut Dog` → `shares mut Animal`
    w: weakref Animal = weakref d         # nor `weakref Dog` → `weakref Animal`
findings.why: [TYP-5] rule 8: "a value to an interface its type implements, keeping the word that says who owns it: a value read in place to `dyn I`, an `owns T` to `owns dyn I`, a `shares T` to `shares dyn I`, a `shares mut T` to `shares mut dyn I`; and a class object to a base class (upcast)". The interface half keeps the word; the base-class half names the plain object only, so an implementer must decide the other words (and `thread_shared`, and `ref`).
findings.proposed_text: In rule 8 replace "and a class object to a base class (upcast)" with "and a class object to a base class (upcast), with its word kept: a `Dog` to an `Animal`, a `shares Dog`, `shares mut Dog`, `thread_shared Dog`, `weakref Dog` or `ref Dog` to the same word on `Animal`; never the reverse, which is a kind test or a cast (`[TYP-44]`)".

findings.title: The `ThreadShared` row names `ref mut` and not `MutSpan`
findings.program:
struct Buf:
    data: MutSpan[int]      # not `ref mut` by name, so "every component is ThreadShared" is read as: a pointer and a length

fn main():
    xs = [1, 2, 3]
    b = thread_shared Buf(data=ref mut xs.as_mut_span())   # `[THR-8]`'s `Send` row treats MutSpan as ref mut; the ThreadShared row is silent
findings.why: Marker table, `ThreadShared`: "`ref mut`, `sharedref mut`, `Cell`, `UnsafeCell`, raw pointers, a `shares` or `shares mut` value and a `weakref` link to one are not (`[THR-9]`)"; the `Send` row names "`ref mut T` and `MutSpan[T]`" together. A `MutSpan` is `ref mut` to each element and belongs in the same list; [TYP-43] says the compiler's own types are "recognised by the module that declares them", so an implementer cannot fall back on a raw-pointer field inside `MutSpan`.
findings.proposed_text: In the `ThreadShared` row: "`ref mut`, `MutSpan`, `sharedref mut`, `Cell`, `UnsafeCell`, raw pointers, a `shares` or `shares mut` value and a `weakref` link to one are not (`[THR-9]`)"; the same word in `[THR-9]`'s list.

findings.title: `String using A` is `E2114` by the closed list, yet a `String` is named among the values made in an arena
findings.why: [TYP-46]: "`using A` after a type whose value has heap memory of its own ... It may follow an `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` type, a class type, or an `Array`, a `Map` or a `Set`; after any other type it is `E2114`". [ALC-1]: "a value that grows (an `Array`, `Map`, `Set` or `String`) made in it keeps the word". A `String` has heap memory of its own and is made in an arena by [ALC-1], and refused by [TYP-46].
findings.proposed_text: In `[TYP-46]` and `[ALC-1]`: "or an `Array`, a `Map`, a `Set` or a `String`" (IV.1 names these as the collection category, "from the memory manager its type names (`[TYP-46]`)").

findings.title: `String` has `+` and "implements none of" the operator interfaces
findings.why: [TYP-21]: "A type has an operator only by implementing its interface (`[TYP-40]`) ... `bool`, `char` and `String` implement none of them (`String`'s `+` takes its left operand over, `[TXT-11]`)". The one sentence both denies `String` the interface and gives it the operator; `Add.add` reads `this` in place, so `String`'s `+` cannot be `Add`'s.
findings.proposed_text: Replace "`bool`, `char` and `String` implement none of them (`String`'s `+` takes its left operand over, `[TXT-11]`)" with "`bool` and `char` implement none of them; `String` implements none either, and its `+` is a built-in of the language, as the scalar operators are: `a + b` takes `a` over and appends `b` (`[TXT-11]`), so `T: needs Add` is not met by `String`".

findings.title: Contextual keywords the grammar uses and [LEX-15] does not list: `module`, `package`, `read`
findings.why: [LEX-15]: "The table above is the complete reserved set. **Contextual keywords** are keywords only in the stated position and identifiers everywhere else: ... `language` and `threads` after `#!` ...". The grammar's `directive` has `"module"` and `visibility` has `"package"` and `"read"`, which the list leaves out.
findings.proposed_text: Add to `[LEX-15]`'s list: "`language`, `threads` and `module` after `#!` (and `main`, `any`, `creator` after `#! threads` are plain identifiers); `package` and `read` inside the round brackets after `pub`".

findings.title: Three literal edges the lexer must guess: `t.0.1`, `-128i8`, `\u{…}` in a byte string
findings.program:
fn main():
    t = ((1, 2), 3)
    x = t.0.1                # `.0.1`: maximal munch reads FLOAT `0.1` after `.`, and `postfix := "." INT` has no match
    m = -128i8               # [LEX-24] covers an untyped literal; `128i8` alone is E2010, so with the suffix the sign has nowhere to apply
    b = b"\u{1F600}"         # [LEX-26]: a byte string holds "ASCII characters or escapes"; `escape` includes `\u{…}`, which is no byte
findings.why: [LEX-18]: "`1.` followed by an identifier character is a method call on `1`; `1.0` is a float" says nothing of a digit after `.` in a field access. [LEX-24]: "A unary minus applied directly to an untyped integer literal forms a negative constant of the literal's eventual type" (untyped only). [LEX-26]: "a byte or C string ASCII characters or escapes" with `escape` holding `\u{…}`.
findings.proposed_text: `[LEX-18]`: add "After `.` the lexer reads an integer, never a float: `t.0.1` is two field accesses." `[LEX-24]`: add "The same holds for a suffixed literal: `-128i8` is the constant −128 of type `i8`; `128i8` without the minus is `E2010`." `[LEX-26]`: replace "a byte or C string ASCII characters or escapes" with "a byte or C string ASCII characters and the escapes but `\u{…}` (`E0009`: "a byte string holds bytes; write the UTF-8 bytes, `\xF0\x9F\x98\x80`, or a text literal")".

findings.title: After F6 the allocation of a shared local is on the making line, and [PHIL-2] still names `shares x`
findings.program:
fn main():
    items = [1, 2, 3]            # [RC-1] (0.9.20): made in a block of its own from this line, "as if that line had said shares"
    v = ref items
    other = shares mut items     # [PHIL-2]: the allocating form is "a value made shared (`shares x`, ...)"; `ember inspect --alloc` lists which line?
findings.why: [PHIL-2]: "The allocating forms are: ... a value made shared (`shares x`, `shares mut x`, `thread_shared x`, `[RC-1]`)". [RC-1]: "a value that is not a class object is then made in a block of its own from the line that made it, as if that line had said `shares`, so nothing moves". The allocation is at the making line; [PHIL-2] and `ember inspect --alloc` point at the sharing line.
findings.proposed_text: In `[PHIL-2]`: "a value made shared (`shares x`, `shares mut x`, `thread_shared x`): the block is made where the value is made, so for a local some later line of the function shares, the allocation is the local's own line (`[RC-1]`), and `ember inspect --alloc` lists that line".

findings.title: A shebang line is an unknown directive
findings.program:
#!/usr/bin/env ember        # [LEX-10]: a line beginning `#!` before the imports is a directive; [GRM-37]: "an unknown directive ... is E0104"
println("hi")               # a script ([FN-8]) that the shell cannot run
findings.why: [LEX-10] and [GRM-37] make every leading `#!` line a directive of three forms; `[FN-8]` calls a file of statements a script, and no rule drops the Unix shebang.
findings.proposed_text: Add to `[LEX-10]`: "A first line beginning `#!` whose next character is `/` is a shebang line, dropped before tokenisation and never a directive, so a script runs from the shell; the formatter keeps it as it is."

findings.title: `extend_decl` takes a `type_body`, which admits fields
findings.program:
struct P:
    x: int

extend P implements Display:
    y: int = 0                     # type_body := NEWLINE INDENT {member} DEDENT; member := ... field_decl ...: parses; no rule says what a field in an `extend` block is
    fn fmt(ref mut f: Formatter) -> Result[void, FmtError]: return f.write(this.x)
findings.why: III.2: "`extend_decl := ["unsafe"] "extend" [generic_params] type [implements] [where_clause] ":" type_body`" and "`member := {attribute} [type_params] [visibility] (field_decl | fn_decl | const_decl | type_alias | "pass" NEWLINE)`". [GRM-34] and [IFC-2] speak of methods and implementations only; a field here is `E0901` by silence, which an implementer may not notice.
findings.proposed_text: Grammar: `extend_decl := ["unsafe"] "extend" [generic_params] type [implements] [where_clause] ":" NEWLINE INDENT {extend_member} DEDENT` with `extend_member := {attribute} [type_params] [visibility] (fn_decl | const_decl | type_alias | "pass" NEWLINE)`. Add to `[GRM-34]`: "An `extend` block adds methods, constants and associated types; a field in one is `E0100` ("an `extend` block adds no field; write `y: int = 0` in `struct P:`")."

findings.title: Whether `a, b = e` declares a name not in scope is unsaid
findings.program:
fn main():
    q = 0
    q, r = divmod(7, 2)       # `q` is in scope and is assigned; `r` is not: declared ([GRM-4] speaks of `x = e` with one name), or E1010?
    println(r)
findings.why: [GRM-4]: "`x = e` where no `x` is in scope declares `x` with the type of `e`; where `x` is in scope it assigns". [GRM-5]: "`a, b = e` destructures a tuple, a struct or a fixed array. The right side is evaluated once". Neither says that each target of a `target_list` follows [GRM-4] on its own.
findings.proposed_text: Add to `[GRM-5]`: "Each target follows `[GRM-4]` on its own: a name not in scope is declared with its part's type, one in scope is assigned (`a, b = b, a` swaps two names in scope; `q, r = divmod(7, 2)` declares both); `_` discards its part."

findings.title: "there is no other view container" reads against `[TYP-15]`'s `Array[StrView]`
findings.program:
fn main():
    names: Array[StrView] = ["ann", "bob"]     # [TYP-15]: a list of views, legal; [TYP-15a]: "there is no other view container"
findings.why: [TYP-15a]: "The arena-backed containers (`ArenaArray`, `ArenaMap`, §IX.2) may hold views bounded by the container's own region (`[ARN-5]`); there is no other view container." [TYP-15]: "A view may be stored in any place — a local, a field of a view type, a list's elements". The sentence means no other container bounds its views by its own region; read alone it denies `Array[StrView]`.
findings.proposed_text: Replace "there is no other view container" with "no other container bounds the views it holds by its own region: an `Array[StrView]` holds views bounded by what each points into (`[TYP-15]`)".

verdicts.reason: [TYP-22]: 'An interface is usable as `dyn` only if every method has an object (none is a `static fn`), does not return `Self` by value (methods marked `where Self: needs Sized` excepted), and is not generic, except over a type parameter used only as the type of a parameter that views its value'. [IFC-5] adds only the generic case: 'an interface whose generic method returns or stores its type parameter is not usable as `dyn`'. [STR-7] defines `Self` 'Inside the body of a `struct`, `enum`, `class` or `extend` block' and nowhere for a call through `dyn I`. So `Same` with `fn same(other: Self)` meets every condition of [TYP-22], `a.same(b)` on two `dyn Same` gives `other` a type no rule names, and the one place that knows the problem is [TYP-36]'s special entry ('`owns dyn I` compares when `I` requires `Eq` ... values of two different kinds are never equal'). Nothing refuses the program; an implementer who reads `Self` as `dyn I` lets one kind's bytes be read as another's.
verdicts.better_fix: The reader's replacement in [TYP-22] is right and general. Add two sentences so that required interfaces are covered too, since [TYP-22] already keeps an interface requiring `Clone` (whose `clone` returns `Self`) usable: 'A method of an interface that `I` requires (`interface Shape: needs (Eq, Ord):`) is reached through `dyn I` only where it names `Self` nowhere but as `this`, and through the two entries this document gives: `clone` (section IX.1) and `eq` ([TYP-36], the kinds compared first). Any other such method called through a `dyn I` value is `E2050` at the call ("`cmp` takes `other: Self`, and through a `dyn Shape` the kind of `other` is unknown; test the kinds first, `if a is Circle as x:` and inside it `if b is Circle as y:`, and call `x.cmp(y)`").' Keep the reader's `E2050` example for `Same` and the `where Self: needs Sized` escape ('which a `dyn` value does not have', the `Sized` row of the marker table).

verdicts.reason: [ENM-3] already answers the direction and the way back: 'A unit-only enum ... converts to its representation with `as`, and converts back with `Mode.from_repr(x) -> Option[Mode]`', so the text does not admit `7 as Color` as a checked program's form and names the checked construction. What remains: [TYP-6] lists its pairs ('integer -> integer: keeps the low bits ...') with no closing sentence for every other pair, and [TYP-12] ('A unit-only enum is an integer') lets an implementer put the enum under [TYP-6]'s first bullet; `bool` under `as` is in neither, so it is E0901 by the document's convention rather than a defined refusal. The proposed help is also wrong against the text: the enum's checked conversion is `Color.from_repr(7) -> Option[Color]` ([ENM-3]), not `try_from`/`RangeError`, which [TYP-6] gives for integers.
verdicts.narrowed_to: [TYP-6] lacks a closing clause for unlisted pairs (an integer to an enum, anything to or from `bool`), and [TYP-12]'s 'is an integer' should read 'is stored as an integer', with [ENM-3] cited.
verdicts.better_fix: In [TYP-12]: 'A unit-only enum is stored as an integer (`@repr(u8)` ...); its values are its variants, and the conversions are [ENM-3]'s.' Add to the end of [TYP-6]'s list: '* `bool -> integer`: `true` is 1 and `false` 0 (Python's `int(True)`, [PHIL-14]); nothing converts to `bool` (`x != 0` is the test); * a unit-only enum -> an integer type that holds every one of its discriminants (`Color.Green as u8`, [ENM-3]); an integer never converts to an enum, since a value of an enum is one of its variants and `Option[Color]` keeps `None` in an unused discriminant ([TYP-13]): `7 as Color` is `E2020` ("an integer may be no `Color`; write `Color.from_repr(7)`, an `Option[Color]`, and open it: `if Color.from_repr(7) exists as c:`"); * `as` between any other pair of types is `E2020`, naming both.'

verdicts.reason: [TYP-46]/[ALC-1]: 'A value whose manager may have several instances keeps its instance's address, one word, so that its growth and its end go back to the instance it came from'. [THR-8]'s reachable list is closed and does not name it: 'nothing reachable from it (its fields, its elements, what its `owns` parts hold, a function value's state) is a one-thread owner ...; collections and class objects are `Send` when every component is'. [ALC-5] makes growth a change of the instance ('the instance is changed only by what allocates from it ...: the `Allocator` methods that value's growth and end call'), and [ARN-1] makes `Arena`'s allocation a change of `this` ('called through a name that may change the arena'). [THR-11] checks 'two of them changing one place' from 'its body and every function it may run', and nothing says a value's growth is a change of its instance for that check, so two scoped tasks growing `xs` and `ys` made in one `Arena` bump one cursor from two threads, and `thread_shared T using A` ends on any thread ([RC-4]) through `deallocate` on a one-thread instance. The text covers neither route.
verdicts.better_fix: The reader's 'a view of its instance, `ref A`, for every rule of the language' would collide with [ALC-5] and [ARN-1]: `allocate` changes the arena, so two values each holding a `ref A` and growing through it would be two changers through read-only views (`E3023`) on one thread, which [ALC-5] deliberately allows. Narrow it to the two rules that need it. Add to [TYP-46] (and the same to [ALC-1] after verdict 107's two exceptions, which stay): '* `[TYP-46a]` **A value made in an instance follows its manager between threads.** For `Send` and `ThreadShared` a value whose growth or end calls its instance's methods (one that keeps the instance word, and one in a `FoundByAddress` manager, whose end finds the instance from its address) holds a `ref A` to that instance: it is `Send`, and `ThreadShared`, only when `A` is `ThreadShared` ([THR-8], [THR-9]), since those calls run on whichever thread holds or ends it. A value made in a manager that frees nothing one by one and does not grow holds nothing. `thread_shared T using A` with an `A` that is not `ThreadShared` is `E7015` at the making line ("`st` would end on whichever thread holds its last owner, and `current`, an `Arena`, is used by one thread; make it in the built-in manager, `st = thread_shared Stats()`, or in a manager any thread may call"). For [THR-11] a value's growth and end are changes of its instance, so two scoped tasks growing values made in one instance are `E7007` naming the instance ("the tasks on lines 7 and 9 grow `xs` and `ys`, both made in `current`, so both change `current`; give each task an arena of its own, `a = Arena(1 << 20)` inside its function, or make the lists in the built-in manager, `xs = []`"), unless `A` is `ThreadShared`. For the exclusivity rules [ALC-5] stands: growth and end are the changes of the instance it allows.' Add `ref A` for such values to the `Send` and `ThreadShared` rows of the marker table.

verdicts.reason: III.3: '`base_type := path_type | "ref" ["mut"] base_type | "sharedref" "mut" base_type | "owns" base_type | "shares" ["mut"] base_type | "thread_shared" base_type | "weakref" base_type | ...`' is recursive on every word. [TYP-45] defines each word over a plain `T` ('`owns T`: held alone, in a heap block of its own ...; `shares T` and `shares mut T`: one of several owners of a value ...') and never a word over a worded type; [TYP-15] names where a view may be stored ('a local, a field of a view type, a list's elements, a struct a call makes') and not an `owns` block or a counted block; [GRM-3] says only that the words 'say who owns the value, how it may be reached and where its memory comes from'. The audit's O2 names `weakref thread_shared T` and `weakref shares T` as the one pair with a meaning or a refusal to decide, and no sentence covers `owns owns T`, `shares mut ref mut T`, `owns ref T` or `thread_shared shares T`. The program parses and no rule says what the two `shares mut` owners of one `ref mut` may do.
verdicts.better_fix: The reader's [TYP-45a] is the right shape with three edits. (1) Leave `weakref thread_shared T` to O2 explicitly ('whether `weakref` stands before `thread_shared T` is [O2]'s question, open with the owner') rather than refusing it, since [THR-8] and [WK-12] need the link's type to say its target's kind. (2) `ref` and `ref mut` stand before an owner word or a link (`ref mut owns Mesh`, `ref weakref Node`: the view of a place that holds such a value, read through by [TYP-14], and `=` on the `ref mut` one replaces what the place holds, as `e.mesh = owns Mesh(...)` does), never before `ref`, `ref mut` or `sharedref mut`: `ref ref T` and `ref mut ref mut T` are `E0100` ("a view of a view names the same place; write `ref mut T`"). Everything else in the proposal (every other word before a word is `E0100`, with the help giving the one-word type; a value that is to hold a view or a link is a struct with such a field) stands.
